chapters.title: The Glory of Kings
chapters.html:
Reproof (Tegsat) 1

1These also are proverbs of Solomon,
which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied.

2It is the glory of God to conceal a matter,
but the glory of kings to search out a matter.

3As the heavens for height and the earth for depth,
so the heart of kings is unsearchable.

4Take away the dross from the silver,
and a vessel comes out for the smith;

5take away the wicked from before the king,
and his throne will be established in righteousness.

6Do not put yourself forward in the king's presence
or stand in the place of the great,

7for it is better to be told, "Come up here,"
than to be put lower in the presence of a noble.
What your eyes have seen

8do not bring hastily into court,
or what will you do in the end,
when your neighbor puts you to shame?

9Argue your case with your neighbor himself,
and do not reveal another's secret,

10or he who hears it will bring shame upon you,
and the ill report about you will not go away.

11Like apples of gold in settings of silver
is a word spoken at the right time.

12Like a gold ring or an ornament of fine gold
is a wise reprover to a listening ear.

13Like the cold of snow in the time of harvest
is a faithful envoy to those who send him;
he refreshes the soul of his masters.

14Like clouds and wind without rain
is a man who boasts of a gift he does not give.

15With patience a ruler may be persuaded,
and a soft tongue will break a bone.

16If you have found honey, eat only enough for you,
or you will be filled with it and vomit it.

17Let your foot be seldom in your neighbor's house,
or he will be filled with you and hate you.

18Like a club, a sword or a sharp arrow
is a man who bears false witness against his neighbor.

19Like a broken tooth or a foot that slips
is trust in a treacherous man in the day of trouble.

20Like one who takes off a garment on a cold day, like vinegar on soda,
is one who sings songs to a heavy heart.

21If your enemy is hungry, give him bread to eat,
and if he is thirsty, give him water to drink;

22for you will heap burning coals on his head,
and the LORD will reward you.

23The north wind brings forth rain,
and a secret tongue, angry looks.

24It is better to live in a corner of the housetop
than in a house shared with a quarrelsome wife.

25Like cold water to a weary soul
is good news from a distant land.

26Like a muddied spring or a polluted fountain
is a righteous man who gives way before the wicked.

27It is not good to eat much honey,
nor is it glory to search out one's own glory.

28Like a city broken into and left without walls
is a man without self-control.

Notes

  • The book — in the Ethiopian Bible, Reproof (Tegsat) is a separate book made of what the Hebrew counts as Proverbs 25–31. Its chapters 1–7 are Proverbs 25–31, and its verse numbers are the same. It is rendered from the Hebrew, as Proverbs is, with the same words for wisdom (see Proverbs 1:2–6).

  • v1 "which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied" — scribes of Hezekiah's court, about 700 BC, gathered a further collection of Solomon's sayings (2 Kings 18:1–7).

  • vv6–7 "it is better to be told, 'Come up here'" — Jesus' parable of the wedding guest who takes the lowest place (Luke 14:8–11).

  • v10 "will bring shame upon you" — yechassedkha, from chesed in its rare sense "reproach," as in Proverbs 14:34.

  • v13 "a faithful envoy" — tsir, as in Proverbs 13:17.

  • v20 "like vinegar on soda" — vinegar on neter, natron, fizzes and spoils it; cheerful songs do the same to a grieving heart.

  • vv21–22 — Paul quotes them from the Greek: heap burning coals on his head… overcome evil with good (Romans 12:20–21).

  • v24 — the same words as Proverbs 21:9, and the English there is followed; "quarrelsome" follows the read form midyanim.

  • v27 "nor is it glory to search out one's own glory" — the Hebrew is terse and uncertain, "and searching out their glory, glory"; the line may mean that too much of a good thing, even honor, cloys.

chapters.title: Answer a Fool
chapters.html:
Reproof (Tegsat) 2

1Like snow in summer or rain in harvest,
so honor is not fitting for a fool.

2Like a sparrow in its flitting, like a swallow in its flying,
so a curse without cause comes back on him who speaks it.

3A whip for the horse, a bridle for the donkey,
and a rod for the backs of fools.

4Do not answer a fool according to his folly,
or you will be like him yourself.

5Answer a fool according to his folly,
or he will be wise in his own eyes.

6Whoever sends a message by the hand of a fool
cuts off his own feet and drinks violence.

7Like the legs of the lame, which hang useless,
is a proverb in the mouth of fools.

8Like one who binds a stone in a sling
is one who gives honor to a fool.

9Like a thorn that goes up into the hand of a drunkard
is a proverb in the mouth of fools.

10Like an archer who wounds everyone
is one who hires a fool or hires those who pass by.

11As a dog returns to its vomit,
so a fool repeats his folly.

12Do you see a man who is wise in his own eyes?
There is more hope for a fool than for him.

13The sluggard says, "There is a lion in the road!
A lion in the streets!"

14As a door turns on its hinges,
so does a sluggard on his bed.

15The sluggard buries his hand in the dish;
it wears him out to bring it back to his mouth.

16The sluggard is wiser in his own eyes
than seven men who can answer sensibly.

17Like one who takes a dog by the ears
is one who passes by and meddles in a quarrel not his own.

18Like a madman who throws firebrands,
arrows and death,

19so is the man who deceives his neighbor
and says, "Was I not joking?"

20Where there is no wood, the fire goes out,
and where there is no whisperer, strife ceases.

21As charcoal to hot embers and wood to fire,
so is a quarrelsome man for kindling strife.

22The words of a whisperer are like delicious morsels;
they go down into the inner parts of the body.

23Like silver dross overlaid on earthenware
are burning lips with an evil heart.

24Whoever hates disguises it with his lips
and stores up deceit within him.

25When he speaks graciously, do not believe him,
for there are seven detestable things in his heart.

26Though his hatred be covered with deception,
his wickedness will be exposed in the assembly.

27Whoever digs a pit will fall into it,
and a stone will come back on him who rolls it.

28A lying tongue hates those it crushes,
and a flattering mouth works ruin.

Notes

  • v2 "comes back on him who speaks it" — the read form lo, "to him"; the written form lo, "not," gives "does not come to rest," which most English versions follow. Either way an undeserved curse does not land where it was aimed.

  • vv4–5 "Do not answer a fool… Answer a fool" — set side by side on purpose: there is a time to refuse a fool's terms and a time to expose his folly.

  • v10 "Like an archer who wounds everyone" — one of the hardest verses in the book; rav may be "archer" or "master," and the Greek reads it very differently.

  • v11 "As a dog returns to its vomit" — quoted in 2 Peter 2:22.

  • v13 — nearly the same as Proverbs 22:13; here "a lion in the road," shachal, beside ari.

  • v15 — the same as Proverbs 19:24, with "it wears him out" for "and will not even."

  • v22 — the same as Proverbs 18:8, and the English there is followed.

  • v23 "burning lips" — fervent words of friendship over a hateful heart, like a cheap clay pot glazed with silver dross.

  • v25 "seven detestable things" — to'evot, as in Proverbs 6:16.

  • v27 "Whoever digs a pit will fall into it" — as in Psalm 7:15 and Ecclesiastes 10:8.

chapters.title: Iron Sharpens Iron
chapters.html:
Reproof (Tegsat) 3

1Do not boast about tomorrow,
for you do not know what a day may bring forth.

2Let another praise you, and not your own mouth;
a stranger, and not your own lips.

3A stone is heavy, and sand is weighty,
but a fool's vexation is heavier than both.

4Wrath is cruel, anger is a flood,
but who can stand before jealousy?

5Better is open rebuke
than hidden love.

6Faithful are the wounds of a friend,
but the kisses of an enemy are profuse.

7One who is full tramples on honey,
but to one who is hungry every bitter thing is sweet.

8Like a bird that strays from its nest
is a man who strays from his home.

9Oil and incense make the heart glad,
and the sweetness of a friend comes from his earnest counsel.

10Do not forsake your friend and your father's friend,
and do not go to your brother's house in the day of your calamity;
better is a neighbor who is near than a brother who is far away.

11Be wise, my son, and make my heart glad,
so that I may answer him who reproaches me.

12The shrewd sees evil and hides himself,
but the simple go on and suffer for it.

13Take a man's garment when he has put up security for a stranger,
and hold it in pledge when he puts it up for a foreign woman.

14Whoever blesses his neighbor with a loud voice, rising early in the morning,
will be counted as cursing.

15A continual dripping on a day of steady rain
and a quarrelsome wife are alike;

16whoever restrains her restrains the wind
and grasps oil in his right hand.

17Iron sharpens iron,
and one man sharpens another.

18Whoever tends a fig tree will eat its fruit,
and whoever guards his master will be honored.

19As in water face reflects face,
so the heart of man reflects the man.

20Sheol and Abaddon are never satisfied,
and the eyes of man are never satisfied.

21The crucible is for silver, and the furnace for gold,
and a man is tested by his praise.

22Though you crush a fool in a mortar with a pestle along with grain,
his folly will not depart from him.

23Know well the condition of your flocks,
and give attention to your herds,

24for riches do not last forever,
nor does a crown endure to all generations.

25When the grass is gone and the new growth appears
and the vegetation of the mountains is gathered,

26the lambs will provide your clothing,
and the goats the price of a field;

27there will be enough goats' milk for your food,
for the food of your household
and life for your young women.

Notes

  • v1 "Do not boast about tomorrow" — as in James 4:13–16.

  • v6 "Faithful are the wounds of a friend" — the honest friend's rebuke heals; the enemy's many kisses betray (Matthew 26:48–49).

  • v7 "One who is full tramples on honey" — tavus, "treads underfoot"; "loathe" is kept in this rendering for sheqets.

  • v10 "your father's friend" — the read form re'a; the written form is a spelling variant.

  • vv12, 13 — the same as Proverbs 22:3 and 20:16, and the English there is followed.

  • v15 "A continual dripping" — as in Proverbs 19:13.

  • v19 "As in water face reflects face" — a man sees himself in his own heart, or in the heart of another.

  • v20 "Sheol and Abaddon" — as in Proverbs 15:11; "Abaddon" is the read form.

  • v21 — the first line is the same as Proverbs 17:3a.

  • vv23–27 — a short poem on care of the flock: wealth and crowns pass, but the herd tended year by year feeds the house.

chapters.title: The Righteous Are Bold as a Lion
chapters.html:
Reproof (Tegsat) 4

1The wicked flee when no one pursues,
but the righteous are bold as a lion.

2When a land transgresses, it has many rulers,
but with a man of understanding and knowledge its order will long endure.

3A poor man who oppresses the poor
is a beating rain that leaves no bread.

4Those who forsake the law praise the wicked,
but those who keep the law strive against them.

5Evil men do not understand justice,
but those who seek the LORD understand everything.

6Better is a poor man who walks in his integrity
than one who is crooked in his ways, though he is rich.

7Whoever keeps the law is a son with understanding,
but a companion of gluttons shames his father.

8Whoever increases his wealth by interest and profit
gathers it for one who is gracious to the poor.

9Whoever turns away his ear from hearing the law,
even his prayer is detestable.

10Whoever leads the upright astray into an evil way
will himself fall into his own pit,
but the blameless will inherit good.

11A rich man is wise in his own eyes,
but a poor man who understands will search him out.

12When the righteous triumph, there is great glory,
but when the wicked rise, people hide themselves.

13Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper,
but whoever confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy.

14Blessed is the one who fears always,
but whoever hardens his heart will fall into calamity.

15Like a roaring lion or a charging bear
is a wicked ruler over a poor people.

16A ruler who lacks understanding is a great oppressor,
but whoever hates unjust gain will prolong his days.

17A man burdened with the blood of a life
will be a fugitive until the pit; let no one help him.

18Whoever walks blamelessly will be saved,
but whoever is crooked in his ways will suddenly fall.

19Whoever works his land will have plenty of bread,
but whoever pursues worthless things will have plenty of poverty.

20A faithful man will abound with blessings,
but whoever hurries to be rich will not go unpunished.

21To show partiality is not good,
and for a piece of bread a man will transgress.

22A man with an evil eye hurries after wealth
and does not know that want will come upon him.

23Whoever rebukes a man will afterward find more favor
than one who flatters with his tongue.

24Whoever robs his father or his mother and says, "That is no transgression,"
is a companion to a man who destroys.

25A greedy man stirs up strife,
but whoever trusts in the LORD will be enriched.

26Whoever trusts in his own heart is a fool,
but whoever walks in wisdom will be delivered.

27Whoever gives to the poor will not lack,
but whoever hides his eyes will get many a curse.

28When the wicked rise, people hide themselves,
but when they perish, the righteous increase.

Notes

  • vv4, 7, 9 "the law" — torah without "my" or "your mother's": God's law, as in Psalm 119, so "law" rather than "teaching."

  • v6 — nearly the same as Proverbs 19:1, with "crooked in his ways, though he is rich" for "crooked in speech and is a fool."

  • v8 "by interest and profit" — forbidden among Israelites (Leviticus 25:36–37; Deuteronomy 23:19); the read form is a spelling variant.

  • v9 "even his prayer is detestable" — to'evah, as in Proverbs 15:8.

  • vv12, 28 "people hide themselves" — the two verses frame the chapter's sayings on rulers.

  • v13 "whoever confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy" — as in Psalm 32:3–5 and 1 John 1:9.

  • v16 "whoever hates" — the read form, singular.

  • v19 — the first line is the same as Proverbs 12:11a.

  • v21 "To show partiality is not good" — as in Proverbs 24:23.
